title: Most people believe great victories require great numbers.
paragraphs: Most people believe great victories require great numbers.

A large army.
A powerful leader.
Overwhelming strength.
But one of the most powerful moments in Scripture began with something very different.
Just two men.

In 1 Samuel 14, Israel was paralyzed with fear. The Philistines had superior weapons, superior numbers, and superior military power. Israel’s army was hiding in caves, trembling, discouraged, and unsure of what to do.
Even King Saul, the leader of the nation, was sitting under a tree with his soldiers, waiting.

Waiting for a plan.
Waiting for courage.
Waiting for something to change.
But Jonathan, Saul’s son, saw the moment differently.
Instead of staring at the problem, he looked at the power of God.
And without announcing it to the entire army, Jonathan turned to his armor bearer and said something that reveals the heart of true faith:

“Come, let’s go over to the outpost of those uncircumcised men. Perhaps the Lord will act in our behalf. Nothing can hinder the Lord from saving, whether by many or by few.”
— 1 Samuel 14:6
Think about that.

Jonathan did not say, “We have the numbers.”
He did not say, “We are stronger.”
He said something far deeper.
God is not limited by numbers.
This is the lesson.
So many people delay obedience because they believe they need more support before they can move.

More people.
More approval.
More resources.
More certainty.
But Jonathan teaches us that faith does not wait for the crowd.
Faith moves when it knows God is able.
Notice something powerful about Jonathan’s words.
He says, “Perhaps the Lord will act.”
That statement is not doubt.
It is humility.
Jonathan was not arrogantly assuming victory. He was acknowledging that the outcome belonged to God. But he also understood something important:
God often moves when someone has the courage to step forward.
Jonathan and his armor bearer began climbing the rocky pass toward the Philistine outpost. It was dangerous. They were exposed. The enemy had the higher ground.
From a military perspective, it made no sense.
But from a faith perspective, it made perfect sense.
Because Jonathan knew that God can turn impossible situations into turning points.
And that is exactly what happened.
As Jonathan and his armor bearer attacked, the Lord sent panic into the Philistine camp. Confusion spread through their army. The ground trembled. Chaos erupted among the enemy forces.
What started with two men suddenly became a national victory.
The entire battle shifted.
But notice something important.
The breakthrough did not begin with the whole army.
It began with one man willing to trust God and one man willing to stand beside him.
Sometimes we underestimate the power of one obedient step.

One prayer.
One decision.
One act of courage.
One moment where someone says, “God is able, even if the odds say otherwise.”
The truth is, many people are stuck in life because they keep measuring their possibilities by what they see around them.
Jonathan measured the moment differently.
He didn’t ask, “How many are with us?”
He asked, “Can God do this with few?”
And the answer was yes.
It has always been yes.
Throughout Scripture, God repeatedly works through what seems small:

David with a sling against a giant.
Gideon with only three hundred men.
A young boy’s lunch feeding thousands.
Twelve disciples turning the world upside down.
Again and again, the Bible reminds us that God’s power is not dependent on human abundance.
In fact, sometimes God chooses the small beginning so that His power is unmistakable.
That means your situation may not be as hopeless as it feels.
You may feel outnumbered.
You may feel unsupported.
You may feel like the resources around you are too small to make a difference.
But Jonathan’s story reminds us of something powerful:
God is not weakened by your small beginning.
He is not intimidated by the odds.
He does not need a crowd to begin a breakthrough.
Sometimes the only thing standing between fear and victory is one person who is willing to believe that God can move.
Jonathan stepped forward.
And history changed.
So here is the question this story leaves us with:
What if the breakthrough you are waiting for is on the other side of a step you have been afraid to take?
What if the courage you feel stirring inside you is not reckless—but faith?
What if God is simply waiting for someone to climb?
Jonathan’s story is not just about a battle long ago.
It is a reminder that heaven still honors courageous faith.
Because even today, nothing can hinder the Lord from saving—whether by many or by few.
What do you think is the hardest part about stepping out in faith when you feel like you are standing alone?
Your answer might encourage someone who needs courage today.
